title: astra.registry.publisher/1
description: publishers/<owner>.json — what the registry knows about the ACCOUNT behind a listing, keyed by the GitHub owner of source.repo (`owner`, and any login in `covers`). Hand-written and hand-reviewed. Never derived from a bundle: a plugin's own manifest carries an `author` string the author typed, and a badge keyed on that would be forged by a one-line edit. The owner login keys the badge because it is what the ownership check binds to; the Minice account a binding needs from R4a never keys one (ROLL-47 A2, amended 2026-09-24).

owner.description: The GitHub owner login, matching the file name. Compared case-insensitively against the owner half of every listing's source.repo.

covers.description:
Further owner logins this ONE record speaks for — an organisation the publisher runs, an account they also publish from. Listings under any of them resolve to this record, so the badge, the display name and the byline are written once and cannot disagree between them.

Why this exists rather than a second file: the badge is keyed on the owner half of source.repo, and a person's plugins do not all live under their personal login. `KnlCE` publishes `astra-chess` from the `KNICE-TECH` organisation, so the reviewed record about the PERSON reached none of their listings while being entirely correct. A second record for the org would have carried the same display_name and tripped the collision check — correctly, because two records rendering as one word IS the thing that check is for. One record, several keys, is the shape that says what is actually true.

What it is NOT: a claim the registry verifies. Nothing here re-fetches an organisation's membership. The claim is this line, in a reviewed commit, exactly as strong as the `owner` line above it and no stronger — and it is worth knowing that it extends the badge to every repository under that owner, including one a collaborator pushes. Add an org you would vouch for as a whole; the narrower knob is to leave this out and let each account carry its own record.

owner_ids.description:
Contract B.4 (2.5.0), OPTIONAL: each login this record speaks for — `owner`, and any login in `covers` — mapped to that account's GitHub numeric id as a base-10 string, read from `GET /users/<login>` and added only by a reviewed commit. The signer's badge join reads it (registry plan TRUST-25; tools/build-index.mjs `publisherFor`): a listing that has `plugins/<id>/identity.json` takes this record's badge only when `owner_ids[<the login it is published under>]` equals that identity record's `repository_owner_id`, and a record with no such entry gives it none. A listing with no identity record keeps the join by login.

WHY A NUMBER BESIDE A NAME. A login is a string its owner can give away: `KNICE-TECH` was freed by an organisation rename and is registrable by anybody. A badge joined by login alone is a badge whoever registers a freed login inherits, on the first bound listing they publish. The numeric id does not move with the name and is never reissued, and the identity record pins the one the binding proved — so the two agreeing is the claim "the account this record was reviewed for is the account that bound this listing".

A STRING, NOT A NUMBER, for the reason schema/identity-v1.json gives: §0.7's canonical base-10 digit string, never coerced. GitHub ids are past 2^31 and a JSON number is a double. The join compares strings, so a number here matches nothing, which fails closed.

WHAT THE SCHEMA CANNOT SAY and tools/validate.mjs does: every key is a login this record speaks for (`owner` or a `covers` entry), compared case-insensitively as logins are, and no login appears twice in two cases. `maxProperties` is `owner` plus `covers`' eight. Nothing re-fetches these ids: like `covers`, the claim is the reviewed line and no stronger. `signed.publishers` never carries them and stays keyed by login (ID-51).

display_name.description: What a person sees beside the badge. One record per publisher rather than a copy per listing, so a rename is one edit and two entries cannot disagree.

description_text.description: One line a PERSON reads beside the badge, saying who this publisher is to Astra — 'Main developer of Astra', not 'verified'. The tier says what kind of claim the registry is making; this says what the publisher actually is, which is the thing a user wanted to know. Reviewed like everything else in this file: it is free text rendered next to a trust mark, which is precisely where an impersonation would want to live, and the only thing standing in front of it is that a human wrote this line and a root-delegated key signed it.

tier.description:
A STRING and not a proto enum, deliberately — a new tier should cost a registry edit and a locale key, not a proto change and an arm in every shell. A client MUST render on explicit membership and never on a value being present or non-default.

`astra_team` and not `official`, because `official` is relative to nothing. Beside a plugin that plays DOOM or renders Bad Apple!!, a reader completes the sentence with the SUBJECT — "the official DOOM plugin", or worse, a claim on somebody else's rights. Naming Astra leaves nothing to complete: it says whose team, which is the only thing this tier ever meant.

verified_at.description: When the evidence below was first accepted.

last_confirmed_at.description: When it last held. Written by the re-check, not by hand.

expires_at.description: The backstop for a re-check that has been failing quietly. A record past this date is dropped from the index, so a tier nobody has confirmed inside the window lapses rather than persisting on the strength of having once been true. Required for `verified`; meaningless for `official`, whose evidence is a file in this repository.

evidence.description: WHY the tier holds, as a fact that can be re-checked later rather than a verdict recorded once. A tier granted and never revisited becomes a claim about who somebody used to be, and this registry is the only place that can notice.

oneOf.description: For `astra_team`: the account belongs to the project. Re-checkable by construction — the claim is this file, in this repository, and changing it is a reviewed commit.

proof.description: A URL on that domain serving the owner login. Re-fetched on a schedule; when it stops naming the owner, the tier is withdrawn. `^https://` rather than `format: "uri"`: `format` is an annotation in 2020-12 and asserts nothing even where it is understood, and tools/lib/jsonschema.mjs does not implement it at all — so it sat here enforcing nothing until a domain-verified publisher arrived, at which point the validator would have THROWN rather than reported. `^https://` is the spelling every other URL field in schema/ uses, and the reason is version-v1.json's: the daemon refuses plaintext before a byte leaves.

oneOf.description: For `verified`: the publisher controls a domain that names them back. The evidence is live, so the badge can be taken away by the world changing rather than only by a person deciding.
